# Yelp Inc. (YELP) — Interrogator Forensic Dossier

*Six consecutive earnings calls reviewed: Q1 2025 (2025-05-08) through Q1 2026 (2026-05-08). Financials from the screener scan (FY2021–FY2025 trajectory) plus TTM/latest-quarter overrides as of 2026-03-31.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has quietly but decisively shifted from **"resilient two-sided local-ad platform"** to **"AI transformation that will reaccelerate a structurally stalling core."** That shift is the whole dossier.

- **Q1 2025** opened confidently: "8% year-over-year revenue growth and strong profitability," Services "16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth," RR&O (Restaurants, Retail & Other) merely "challenging." AI was a feature layer (Yelp Assistant, photo recognition, answering services "coming soon"). The frame was *growth with a soft pocket*.
- By **Q2 2025** the soft pocket widened: revenue growth decelerated to **4%**, RR&O **-5%**, and even Services growth halved from 14% to **8%**. Management introduced the **data-licensing / AI-search API** narrative ("API calls up 20x over the past year… $10M annual run rate") — the first new growth driver bolted on to offset core deceleration.
- **Q3 2025**: revenue +4% again, RR&O -2%, Services +7%, ad clicks now **-11% YoY**. The DoorDash partnership (food ordering) and the Yelp Host/Receptionist voice-SaaS products are introduced. Adjusted EBITDA actually *declined* 3% YoY for the first time in the window.
- **Q4/FY2025**: the pivot is now explicit and capitalized into a three-pillar 2026 strategy — (1) conversational Yelp Assistant, (2) AI SaaS for businesses (Hatch acquisition closed, Yelp Host), (3) data licensing across the AI ecosystem (OpenAI deal signed). RR&O revenue fell **-6%** for the full year.
- **Q1 2026** is the tell: total revenue **+1% YoY**, RR&O ad revenue **-11%**, Services ad revenue **+1%** (services has now effectively stalled too), paying locations **-6% to 485k**, net income **-27% YoY**, adjusted EBITDA **-7%**. The *only* thing growing is **Other revenue +75%** (Hatch inclusion + licensing + food ordering). Management reframes the entire business around a **$250M other-revenue run-rate target by end-2028** (vs ~$116M run-rate in Q1-26).

**Growth drivers introduced then leaned on harder each quarter:** Yelp Assistant (project share 5%→15%), data licensing (OpenAI, Apple Maps, Bing, Alexa, Meta.ai), Yelp Host (1.5M-call annual run-rate by April 2026), Hatch ($34M ARR, +92%). **Quietly contracting:** the core advertising engine — paying locations have fallen every single quarter (517k→515k→512k→…→485k), ad clicks have been negative all six quarters and are accelerating downward (-3%→-7%→-11%→-10%), and the headline revenue growth rate collapsed from 8% to 1% across five quarters. The narrative has gotten *richer* (more product names, bigger TAMs) precisely as the financial base got *poorer*. That is the classic shape of a management team out-talking a decelerating core.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Mgmt claim | Quarter | Hard number | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Services… 16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth" | Q1-25 | Services +14%, but +8% by Q2-25, +7% Q3-25, **+1% Q1-26** | **Diverges** — the growth engine the whole thesis rested on decelerated to a stall in 12 months |
| "strong profitability… margin potential" | all | Net margin 7%→12%→10%→5%; FY25 NI +10%; **Q1-26 NI -27% YoY** | **Mixed** — FY-level profitability real, but the latest quarter shows margin compression as they spend into the pivot |
| "record net revenue" | Q2/Q3-25 | True quarter-on-quarter, but FY25 rev only **+4%** and Q1-26 **+1%** | **Technically true, narratively misleading** — "records" mask a 1% growth rate |
| "disciplined expense management… flat headcount" | all | FCF margin 22%, TTM FCF $281M, P/FCF 4.7x | **Matches** — this is the genuinely strong part; the cash engine is real |

| "other revenue… $250M run-rate by 2028" | Q1-26 | Other rev +75% to $29M/qtr (~$116M run-rate); needs ~2.2x in <3 yrs | **Aspirational** — credible given Hatch's $34M ARR +92% and licensing, but it is replacing, not adding to, a shrinking ad base |

**Net read:** the cash-generation and capital-return claims are fully corroborated by the numbers — this is a real FCF machine buying back a fifth of itself. But the *growth* narrative is materially richer than the trajectory justifies: every forward-looking driver management emphasizes (AI search, voice SaaS, Hatch) is being marshalled to explain why a +1% top line will someday reaccelerate, while the core ad business shrinks on paying-location count, clicks, and now even Services.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Declining (on the core) / Pivoting (on the narrative).**

- **Q1-25 (offensive):** "continued strength," "strong momentum," "excited by the opportunities." Confident, growth-forward.
- **Q2-25 (first defensive notes):** "advertisers exercised increased caution," "did not see the seasonal increase we would typically expect," macro invoked repeatedly. Tone tilts to explaining absence of growth.
- **Q3-25 (defensive + reframing):** "heightened macroeconomic uncertainties will persist," EBITDA *down* 3%, but heavy pivot language — "Yelp's transformation with AI continues to accelerate," 35 new features. Offense rhetorically, defense financially.
- **Q4-25 (full pivot):** the word "transform"/"transformation" dominates; "we plan to increase our investments in 2026." Management is now selling a *future* business.
- **Q1-26 (defensive core, aggressive pivot):** "local businesses have continued to face a challenging economic environment," NI -27%, and the new framing device — a 2028 other-revenue target — to redirect attention away from a +1% quarter and a -11% RR&O. Note the late mention of "the conflict in the Middle East" / "dynamics… in March" as a fresh macro excuse.

The CPC mechanic is a recurring rhetorical shield: clicks fall double-digits, CPC rises double-digits, and management frames this as "delivering fewer but higher-quality clicks" and "advertiser demand outpacing consumer demand." That is partly true (services mix), but it is also how a platform whose *consumer engagement is shrinking* (app unique devices -2% YoY, "consumers visited restaurants with reduced frequency") describes monetizing a declining audience harder.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High (on hitting/beating the printed guide) — but the guide itself has been serially lowered.**

- The screener records **7/7 quarterly beats (100%)**, and the calls corroborate a consistent beat-and-raise *cadence* on the bottom line: Q1-25 EBITDA "$15M above the high end," Q2-25 "$11M above," Q3-25 "$13M above," Q1-26 EBITDA "$15M above the high end." - BUT the **full-year revenue guide was cut through the year**: FY25 revenue guided to $1.465–1.485B (Q1-25) → narrowed to $1.465–1.475B (Q2) → *lowered* to $1.460–1.465B (Q3). They beat the *lowered* bar. That is sandbag-and-beat on a declining trajectory, not genuine upside.
- So: **High reliability on the printed number, Medium on the trajectory.** They reliably clear a bar they keep setting lower. The EBITDA beats are real and partly mechanical (capitalized software development was explicitly cited as a Q1-26 EBITDA tailwind — a quality-of-earnings caveat).

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **"What needs to change for RR&O to stabilize?"** (KeyBanc, Raymond James, Baird recurring). Management's answer never changes: it's "macro," in-restaurant dining "will return," they're "well positioned." Two-plus years of the same answer while RR&O goes from -3% to -11%. The non-answer is the answer: they have no lever on the structural side.
- **OpenAI / data-licensing visibility** (BofA, Q1-26, pointed): "when I search for restaurants on ChatGPT today, Yelp content appears relatively limited versus Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor… what needs to happen for Yelp to become more visible?" Stoppelman *cannot answer* — "we can't really comment on that nor do we have all the details of their plans." The load-bearing AI-distribution story is outside Yelp's control and management admits it.
- **Hatch margin / contribution** (multiple): management deflects to "growth not margin is the focus," and flags that retention payments are being *added back* to adjusted EBITDA — a real quality-of-earnings caution analysts surfaced.
- **Yelp Assistant → actual paid-lead conversion / ROI** (Baird, Q1-26): asked directly whether assistant-driven projects convert and lift advertiser ROI materially differently; answer was qualitative ("we feel really good," "early signs are really good"), no conversion metric. The engagement stat (15% of RaQ projects) is an activity metric, not a revenue metric.

The throughline: analysts keep probing whether the AI/other-revenue story is *incremental and monetizable* or merely *replacing* a shrinking ad base, and management's answers are consistently directional and TAM-flavored rather than quantified.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Paying advertising locations down every quarter** — 517k → 515k → 512k → … → **485k** (Q1-26, -6% YoY). The customer base of the core business is eroding, not just its spend.

🔴 **Net income -27% and adjusted EBITDA -7% in Q1-26** — the pivot is now visibly costing current profitability.
🔴 **Insider open-market activity: 0 buys vs 33 sells (476,663 sh)** — zero real conviction from people who know best; the scan's positive buy_ratio is grant-inflated and false.

🟢 **Genuine cash machine** — 90% gross margin, 22% FCF margin, TTM FCF $281M, P/FCF 4.7x, net debt only ~$45M. The balance sheet is clean and the cash is real.
🟢 **Other revenue +75%, Hatch $34M ARR +92%, food ordering +88%** — the new engines are growing fast off a small base; the pivot has *some* traction, not zero.
🟢 **SBC discipline** — SBC/revenue cut to 8% (target <6% by 2027), improving GAAP earnings quality over time.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING** (with a STABLE-to-deteriorating core cash engine underneath).

# YELP Inc. — Forensic Dossier (Interrogator)

*Six consecutive earnings calls reviewed: Q1-2025 (2025-05-08) through Q1-2026 (2026-05-08). Financials cross-referenced against the screener trajectory (FY2021–FY2025) plus the TTM/latest-quarter overrides (as of 2026-03-31).*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management told a year ago and the story it tells today are materially different — not in branding, but in what is actually carrying the business.

**Q1-2025 (the high-water mark of the old story):** Yelp opened the period reporting **8% YoY revenue growth** and an expanding margin, led by Services (+14% YoY, "16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth"). The narrative had two legs: (1) a resilient, high-margin Services advertising engine offsetting a weak Restaurant/Retail & Other (RR&O) book, and (2) AI as an *enhancement* layer — Yelp Assistant driving Request-a-Quote project volume, themed ad formats, better matching. RR&O was a known sore spot (−3% YoY) but framed as cyclical/macro, not structural.

**The deceleration is the spine of the arc.** Watch the headline revenue print degrade call by call: **Q1-25 +8% → Q2-25 +4% → Q3-25 +4% → FY-25 +4% → Q1-26 +1%.** Services advertising, the supposed durable leg, decelerated in lockstep: **+14% (Q1-25) → +8% (Q2-25) → +7% (Q3-25) → +1% (Q1-26).** That last number is the tell — the "resilient" growth engine has converged to flat. RR&O never stopped bleeding: −3% → −5% → −2% (FY −6%) → **−11% in Q1-26**, accelerating *down*, not stabilizing.

**The narrative pivot:** as the ad business flattened, management progressively re-pointed the story at three new pillars introduced and amplified across the year — (a) **AI SaaS products** (Yelp Host call-answering for restaurants, Yelp Receptionist for services, now folded into the **Hatch** acquisition closed Feb-2026), (b) **data licensing** to AI search players (the "$10M run-rate" disclosed Q2-25, then the **OpenAI** agreement headlined Q4-25/Q1-26), and (c) **transaction revenue** via the **DoorDash** food-ordering partnership. By Q1-26 these are bundled as "**other revenue**," which grew **+75% YoY to $29M** — and management has set a flag in the ground: a **$250M other-revenue run-rate target by end-2028**, "more than double" the Q1-26 run-rate.

So the arc is a classic incumbent-in-transition: the core monetization engine (CPC advertising on local-business listings) is decelerating toward zero growth, and a small, fast-growing, lower-visibility set of adjacencies is being promoted to carry the equity story. The question the rest of this dossier interrogates: **is the new leg real and large enough, or is it a $29M tail being asked to do the work of a $1.4B body that is quietly shrinking on a same-store basis?**

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where stated | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Record net revenue… strong profitability" | Q2/Q3-25, FY-25 | FY-25 rev $1.46B (+4%), NI $146M (+10%), EPS $2.24 (+19%) | **True but flattering.** Record revenue is real; but +4% is the *slowest* growth in the 5-yr table (rev CAGR was +7.1%). EPS growth is buyback-driven, not operational. |
| Services is the durable growth engine | every call | Services ad rev +14%→+8%→+7%→**+1%** (Q1-26) | **Decisively breaking.** The "resilient" leg decelerated 14pts in four quarters to flat. The thesis pillar is failing in real time. |
| Margin potential of the business (24–27% adj. EBITDA) | Q1–Q3-25 | Adj. EBITDA margin 24%→27%→26% in 2025, but **22% in Q1-26**; adj. EBITDA −7% YoY, NI −27% YoY Q1-26 | **Reversing.** The margin story peaked mid-2025 and is now contracting as they spend behind Hatch + traffic acquisition. |
| EPS growth is strong (+19% YoY) | FY-25 | Diluted shares cut 86M→67M (−22%) 2021–25; FY-25 EPS +19% | **Engineered, not earned.** Net income +10% but EPS +19% — the gap is the buyback. TTM diluted EPS has already rolled to **$2.18** (below the $2.24 FY print), and Q1-26 latest-Q EPS was **−17% YoY**. The per-share tailwind is decelerating as the price (and thus shares retired per dollar) matters less than the shrinking numerator. |
| CPC strength shows pricing power | Q2/Q3-25, Q1-26 | CPC +9%→+11%→+14%→+8% YoY; ad clicks −3%→−7%→−11%→−10% YoY | **A red flag dressed as strength.** Rising CPC on *falling* clicks is mix/scarcity, not demand. Management itself admits (Q3-25, Schwarzbach) "fewer clicks on the platform… resulted in higher prices." Revenue per click is propping up a platform with shrinking engagement. |
| FCF generation is strong (P/FCF 4.6x) | implied by screener | FY FCF margin 22%; **TTM FCF $281M**; net debt now **+$45M** (was net cash) | **FCF real, but the balance sheet flipped.** The screener's "−299M net debt" (net cash) is STALE. Post-Hatch ($271M cash), the recomputed 2026-03-31 position is **net DEBT $45M** (total debt $155M − cash $110M). The "fortress balance sheet" leg of the value case is materially weaker than the input headline. |
| Other revenue is the future ($250M by 2028) | Q1-26 | Other rev $29M in Q1-26 (~$116M annualized run-rate); +75% YoY | **Real growth, trivial base.** Even if they hit $250M run-rate by end-2028, that is ~$130M of *incremental* revenue spread over ~3 years against a $1.46B base that is flat-to-down. It does not offset a shrinking ad core on any near-term horizon. |
| Paying locations stable | management de-emphasizes | 517k → 515k → 512k → **485k** (Q1-26) | **Quiet erosion accelerating.** −6% YoY in Q1-26 — the customer *count* is leaving, masked by per-location CPC inflation. This is the single most damning operating metric. |

**Bottom line of the forensic:** the screener's value headline (P/FCF 4.6x, 138% margin of safety, net cash, beat 7/7) is built substantially on **stale and backward-looking inputs**. The live picture — flat revenue, decelerating Services, −11% RR&O, −6% paying locations, margin contraction, a balance sheet that flipped to net debt, and TTM EPS already rolling over — is a business whose *current* trajectory is decelerating into the AI-search transition, not a stable cash machine being mispriced for no reason.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: DECLINING (offensive → defensive).**

- **Q1-25 — confident, offensive:** "Led by continued strength in our Services business… 8% growth and strong profitability." Forward-leaning AI-product language ("reinvent the search experience," "take it off of Yelp" as an API). Guidance *raised/widened upward*.
- **Q2-25 — hedging creeps in:** "advertisers exercised increased caution… we did not see the seasonal increase in revenue that we would typically expect." Still record-revenue framing, but the macro caveat moves from footnote to thesis. Narrows full-year revenue range.
- **Q3-25 — defensive, macro-anchored:** RR&O weakness now attributed flatly to "macro… continues to be uncertainty"; Jed Nachman: "the main story there is the macro… at the margins, we see impacts from some of the competitive pressures." Note the *deflection* — competition acknowledged only "at the margins." Full-year revenue range **lowered**.
- **FY-25 / Q1-26 — pivot-and-promise:** the tone shifts from defending the ad business to *selling a new story* — Hatch, Yelp Host, OpenAI, the $250M-by-2028 other-revenue target. This is the classic move: when the core decelerates, management lengthens the horizon and points at a TAM ("over $1 billion in the United States for Yelp Host"). Q1-26: "we expect the operating environment for local businesses to remain challenging this year" — an explicit defensive admission for the full year ahead.

The confidence is being *relocated* from delivered ad results (which are deteriorating) to undelivered AI optionality (which is unproven at scale). That is a declining-confidence signature even though the delivery cadence ("beat guidance again") stays intact.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: HIGH on the short-cycle beat mechanics, but the bar is being lowered.**

Yelp has a genuine, repeatable habit of setting conservative quarterly ranges and beating them — corroborated by the screener's **beat 7/7 (100%)** and visible in the transcripts: Q1-25 revenue "$4M above the high end," adj. EBITDA "$15M above the high end"; Q2-25 "$3M above"/"$11M above"; Q3-25 "$6M above"/"$13M above"; Q1-26 "$6M above"/"$15M above." The EBITDA beats are large and consistent — there is a clear **sandbagging pattern** on the bottom line (they guide cautious opex, then flow outperformance through).

**But two credibility erosions matter:**
1. **The full-year revenue guide was cut intra-year** (Q3-25 lowered to $1.460–1.465B from $1.465–1.485B). Beating a quarterly number you set low while cutting the annual number is not the same as delivering — it is managing the cadence while the trajectory slips.
2. **The 2025 SBC target ("less than 8% by end-2025") was hit (8% in Q1-26), but the next leg ("less than 6% by end-2027") is the load-bearing promise for GAAP profitability — undelivered.** And the EBITDA-margin "potential" narrative (24–27%) was directly contradicted by the Q1-26 print (22%, −7% YoY) the moment they started spending behind Hatch. Management's own margin guidance proved aspirational the first quarter it was tested against real investment.

So: **High** reliability on "we will beat this quarter's modest bar"; **Medium** on "the trajectory is what we imply" — they sandbag the print and lower the destination.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The Q&A reveals exactly where the bodies are, by what management *won't* answer crisply:

- **"What's really driving services deceleration — is it competition or macro?"** (Segura, Q2-25; Witaszek/Baird, Q2-25). Management reflexively answers "macro," repeatedly, and confines competition (food-delivery providers eating restaurants; Google eating local search) to "at the margins." This is the **central deflection** — every quarter analysts probe whether the decline is structural; every quarter management insists it is cyclical. The −11% RR&O and −6% locations in Q1-26 are the bad news that probe foreshadowed.
- **CPC-up / clicks-down** (multiple quarters): analysts repeatedly ask whether rising CPC is healthy. Schwarzbach's Q3-25 answer is candid but unflattering — fewer clicks *cause* higher prices. Analysts are circling the fact that revenue stability is an artifact of scarcity pricing, not demand.
- **OpenAI partnership scope** (Bansal/BofA, Q1-26): the sharpest exchange. Bansal points out that on ChatGPT today "**Yelp content appears relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor**" and asks what makes Yelp primary. Jeremy *cannot answer*: "we can't really comment on… their plans… continue to watch that space." The load-bearing AI-licensing catalyst is one where Yelp has **no control and no visibility** into whether it becomes material.
- **Hatch margin/contribution** (Patel/Raymond James, Q4-25; Bansal, Q1-26): analysts press for the EBITDA impact and contribution; Schwarzbach declines to quantify margin ("driving margin is not the immediate focus") and notes retention payments are *added back* to adjusted EBITDA — a quality-of-earnings caution.

What analysts worry about that management isn't addressing: **whether AI search (Google AI Overviews + ChatGPT) structurally disintermediates Yelp's role as the destination for local discovery** — i.e., whether Yelp becomes a wholesale data supplier (licensing pennies) instead of the retail advertising venue (CPC dollars). Management's answer is to *embrace* the licensing role as upside, but never reconciles it against the cannibalization of the far larger ad business.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Services advertising decelerated from +14% to +1% YoY in four quarters** — the durable-growth pillar is collapsing (Q1-25→Q1-26).
🔴 **Paying advertising locations −6% YoY to 485k** (517k→485k across the year) — customers are leaving; revenue held by CPC inflation, not retention (Q1-26).
🔴 **Ad clicks −10% to −11% YoY** while CPC +8–14% — engagement/traffic is structurally falling; "pricing power" is scarcity pricing (Q2-25→Q1-26).
🔴 **Margin reversed: adj. EBITDA margin 27% (Q2-25) → 22% (Q1-26), adj. EBITDA −7% YoY, NI −27% YoY** the moment they invested behind Hatch (Q1-26).
🔴 **Balance sheet flipped from net cash to net debt $45M** post-Hatch — the "fortress" value-input is stale (2026-03-31).
🔴 **Insider behavior: 0 open-market buys vs 33 sells (476,663 sh)** — no insider is buying the "138% margin of safety."
🔴 **App unique devices −2% YoY** (FY-25) — the consumer funnel itself is shrinking, not just monetization.
🔴 **The load-bearing AI catalysts (OpenAI, data licensing) are third-party-controlled and unquantified** — management explicitly "can't comment" on whether Yelp content becomes primary (Q1-26).

🟢 **Buyback is aggressive and accretive:** diluted shares 86M→67M (−22%, 2021–25); $500M authorization added Feb-2026; repurchasing through the price weakness ($32–37 avg). Real per-share value transfer.
🟢 **Gross margin 90% and FCF margin ~22%** — the unit economics of the legacy platform remain excellent; this is a cash machine, not a cash incinerator.
🟢 **Other revenue +75% YoY** with a credible (if small) diversification roadmap (Hatch +92%, food ordering +88%, licensing) — genuine optionality, real product velocity.
🟢 **Beat 7/7 with large EBITDA beats** — execution discipline and conservative guidance are real.

The flags are asymmetric: the red flags hit the *core, large, current* earnings base; the green flags are either financial engineering (buyback) or a *small, future* adjacency. That asymmetry is the whole investment question.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **Terminology migration: "advertising platform" → "AI transformation."** Across the six calls the self-description shifts from a local-advertising marketplace to "transforming Yelp with AI." When a decelerating incumbent re-labels itself around the very technology threatening it, that is both an offensive bet and a tell that the old label no longer sells.
- **"Other revenue" is being promoted from a footnote to a headline.** A year ago it was barely mentioned; by Q1-26 it has a multi-year run-rate target ($250M by 2028) and leads the prepared remarks. Management is teaching the street to value the stub, not the core — because the core is shrinking.
- **The data-licensing framing is double-edged and management knows it.** They sell OpenAI/Apple/Bing/Meta.ai licensing as validation ("essential partner"). But every one of those surfaces is a venue where a consumer gets the answer *without visiting Yelp* — i.e., the licensing revenue is the toll Yelp collects on its own disintermediation. Jeremy's repeated "we're before the first inning" hedge is doing a lot of work to avoid sizing the cannibalization.
- **Capital-allocation language tightened around acquisitions.** Earlier calls list "returning excess capital" prominently; by FY-25/Q1-26 the first priority becomes "investing in strategic transactions" (Hatch) — a subtle reordering from shareholder return toward empire-building into the AI-SaaS adjacency, where Yelp has no proven edge against far better-capitalized players (a risk Bansal flagged directly in Q1-26).
- **No management changes**, but a notable *constancy*: founder-CEO Stoppelman has run this for ~20 years through every prior "reinvent the search experience" promise. The pattern of perennial product reinvention without revenue inflection is itself a signal.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: DETERIORATING / PIVOTING.** The core local-advertising franchise is in same-store decline (paying locations −6%, Services growth collapsed to +1%, RR&O −11%, clicks −10%), masked at the headline by CPC scarcity-pricing and an aggressive buyback. Management is mid-pivot into AI-SaaS (Hatch) and data licensing — real product velocity, but a base too small ($29M/qtr) and a competitive position too exposed to offset the erosion of the ad core on any horizon the buyback can bridge.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** *Is the cheapness (P/FCF ~5x) a fear-print mispricing of a stable cash machine, or the market correctly discounting a structurally-shrinking local-search franchise being disintermediated by Aic search?* The evidence here leans toward the latter on the **operating trajectory**, partially offset by a still-excellent FCF/buyback that can return capital faster than the base erodes for some years. This is a *melting-ice-cube-with-a-good-air-conditioner* situation, not a clean mispricing — and the input headline ("net cash, 138% MoS, beat 7/7") is built on stale figures that overstate the safety.

**ECONOMIC MOAT.** Moat type: **intangible-brand + two-sided network** (330M reviews, 8M listings, consumer mindshare for "find a local business"). Historically a real moat. **WIDTH judged by the evidence: NARROW and ERODING.** ROIC is **9.0%** — barely above cost of capital, and *falling* as margins compress (adj. EBITDA margin 27%→22%, NI margin 12%→5% Q1-26); ad clicks and unique devices are declining (−10%, −2%), meaning the network's *consumer* side — the source of the moat — is thinning. A moat whose underlying engagement is shrinking and whose returns are compressing is not wide; it is eroding. **MOAT_TREND: ERODING.**

**SECULAR THREAT — TERMINAL vs cyclical.** The threat is **ai-displacement / AI-search disintermediation of local discovery**, and it is **MATERIAL, bordering on terminal.** Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT answer "best taco near me" *in the result*, collapsing the click-through that Yelp monetizes; Yelp's own consumer funnel (unique devices −2%, clicks −10%) is already showing it. Management's strategic response — license the data to the disintermediators — converts a high-margin retail-ad dollar into a low-margin wholesale-licensing penny, a structurally lower-value terminal state even if it "works." This is not a cyclical RR&O dip (management's preferred framing); the Services deceleration to +1% in a *non-recessionary* tape, alongside falling devices, points to structural intent-leakage. The cheapness is therefore **partly a fear-print but primarily a structurally-shrinking base** — a value trap risk, with the buyback (not the operating business) doing the work that keeps it from being a pure trap. The 90% gross margin and FCF buy *time*, not immunity.

---

Over the six quarters in front of us, Yelp's story quietly changed shape — from "a resilient local-advertising machine throwing off cash" to "an advertising business in slow structural decline that is racing to reinvent itself with artificial intelligence."

In early 2025 (first quarter, call dated May 8, 2025) the headline was strength: 8% revenue growth, a Services advertising business compounding at double digits for a sixteenth straight quarter, and management leaning into a "product-led strategy." - **The vocabulary flipped from "advertising" to "AI."** Early calls measured success in locations, clicks, and cost-per-click. Recent calls measure it in "features shipped" (35, then 55), "annual run rate" of calls handled, and partnership logos (Alexa, Apple Maps, Bing, Meta.ai, OpenAI). When a company stops quoting the metrics that pay the bills and starts quoting activity metrics, watch the core.
- **Capitalized software development is doing quiet work.** Management twice noted that more spending is being "capitalized" because of "greenfield projects" — this flatters near-term margins and EBITDA by pushing costs off the current income statement. A subtle quality-of-earnings caution.
- **The Hatch retention payments are added back to adjusted EBITDA** — management disclosed this directly. Adjusted EBITDA is being flattered by excluding real acquisition costs.

**Trajectory: PIVOTING — with a deteriorating core.** This is a company managing a slow structural decline in its advertising franchise by harvesting cash, shrinking the share count, and betting on artificial-intelligence products to eventually refill the growth tank. The buyback is excellent and the cash generation is real; the underlying business is eroding.

The Q1 2026 numbers — Services advertising at +1%, the marketplace being used less each quarter, and management unable to explain how Yelp surfaces inside ChatGPT — tilt toward the second reading. The buyback can compound per-share value for a while even on a shrinking base, but it cannot reverse the secular tide.

**Declining.** The shift from offensive (growth, investment) to defensive (efficiency, macro, "challenging environment") language is unmistakable across the six calls.

- Q1 2025: confident, growth-forward — "continued strength," "16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth."
- Q2 2025: first cracks — "advertisers exercised increased caution," "macroeconomic and policy uncertainties," budgets did not rise "to the same extent as we have seen historically."
- Q3 2025: defensive — lowered the full-year revenue range, ad clicks down 11%, leaned on cost discipline.
- Q4 2025 / Q1 2026: pivot mode — the calls became almost entirely about AI initiatives (Yelp Assistant, Yelp Host, Hatch, OpenAI), with the core advertising decline acknowledged but quickly redirected toward the new story. Guidance flagged "the degree of uncertainty that we need to reflect."

Management is becoming *less* specific about the core business (clicks, locations, RR&O) and *more* enthusiastic about early-stage AI products where there are no hard numbers to be held to yet. That is a classic tell of a management team steering attention away from a decelerating core.

---

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**High on the mechanics, low on the trajectory.** Yelp has a genuine habit of beating its own near-term guidance — the screener shows a 7-of-7 beat rate, and on each call adjusted EBITDA came in above the high end of the outlook range (e.g., Q1 2026 EBITDA was "$15 million above the high end"). This is real and earns credit.

But there is a clear **sandbagging pattern**: they set conservative ranges, beat them, and book the applause — while the *full-year* numbers kept getting *cut* (the full-year revenue range was lowered in Q3 2025; 2026 EBITDA guidance of $310–330M is below 2025's actual $369M). Beating a lowered bar is not the same as the business doing well. Reliability of the quarter-ahead guide: **High.** Reliability of the multi-year growth narrative: **Low** — they have repeatedly described AI products as imminent revenue drivers without yet producing material revenue from them.

---

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

Analysts circled the same wounds for six straight quarters:

- **The OpenAI / AI-search partnership reality.** A Bank of America analyst pressed directly in Q1 2026: "when I search for restaurants... on ChatGPT today, Yelp content appears relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor." Management could not answer — "we can't really comment on that nor do we have all the details of their plans." That is a major non-answer on the most important strategic question.
- **What fixes RR&O?** Repeatedly asked; management consistently fell back on "it's a macro story" and "in-restaurant dining will return," deflecting the competitive-pressure framing (food-delivery players, Google) that analysts kept raising.
- **Rising cost-per-click while clicks fall.** Analysts probed whether higher prices on fewer clicks is healthy or a sign of a shrinking marketplace. Management framed it as "mix" and "value per lead," but the underlying truth — fewer people are clicking — leaked through every quarter (clicks -3%, -7%, -11%, -10%).
- **Hatch / AI-product scale and margin.** Analysts asked repeatedly how big and how profitable; management declined to quantify the contribution to next year, saying margin "is not the immediate focus."

The pattern that later turned into bad news: the soft, deflected answers on RR&O and clicks in 2025 became the 11%-RR&O-decline and 27%-net-income-drop reality of Q1 2026.

---

## 6. Red Flags / Green Flags

🔴 **Core advertising decelerating to a stall** — Services advertising +1%, RR&O advertising -11% in Q1 2026; paying advertising locations down 6% to 485,000.
🔴 **Profit dollars guided down** — 2026 EBITDA guide $310–330M vs $369M actual in 2025; net income -27% YoY in Q1 2026.
🔴 **Falling engagement** — app unique devices down 2% YoY; ad clicks down 10–11% — the marketplace is being used less, propped up only by higher prices.
🔴 **The Google / AI existential question went unanswered** — management could not describe how its content actually shows up in ChatGPT or where it ranks versus rivals.
🔴 **Insider behavior** — open-market activity is zero buys versus 33 sells (~477,000 shares). No insider is putting cash in at these "cheap" prices.

🟢 **Exceptional free cash flow and a clean balance sheet** — $281M trailing free cash flow, only ~$45M net debt; 90% gross margins.
🟢 **Disciplined, aggressive, value-accretive buyback** — count cut ~22% in four years, buying heavily at $24–25, with a fresh $500M authorization. This directly compounds per-share value even with flat revenue.
🟢 **Stock-based compensation falling** — from ~10% to 8% of revenue, on track to under 6% by 2027, improving the *quality* of earnings.
🟢 **Real, if early, AI optionality** — Hatch growing ~90%, "other revenue" up 75%, genuine demand for data licensing from AI players. A free call option if it works.

---

## 7. Hidden Signals

- **The vocabulary flipped from "advertising" to "AI."** Early calls measured success in locations, clicks, and cost-per-click. Recent calls measure it in "features shipped" (35, then 55), "annual run rate" of calls handled, and partnership logos (Alexa, Apple Maps, Bing, Meta.ai, OpenAI). When a company stops quoting the metrics that pay the bills and starts quoting activity metrics, watch the core.
- **Capitalized software development is doing quiet work.** Management twice noted that more spending is being "capitalized" because of "greenfield projects" — this flatters near-term margins and EBITDA by pushing costs off the current income statement. A subtle quality-of-earnings caution.
- **The Hatch retention payments are added back to adjusted EBITDA** — management disclosed this directly. Adjusted EBITDA is being flattered by excluding real acquisition costs.
- **Capital allocation language subtly reordered.** Buybacks moved from the third priority to being framed alongside "strategic transactions" (the Hatch deal) — management is signaling it may spend more on acquisitions and less on buybacks going forward, which would remove the one reliable support under the per-share story.

---

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING — with a deteriorating core.** This is a company managing a slow structural decline in its advertising franchise by harvesting cash, shrinking the share count, and betting on artificial-intelligence products to eventually refill the growth tank. The buyback is excellent and the cash generation is real; the underlying business is eroding.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh:** Is the cheap price (about 4.8x free cash flow) a mispricing of a durable cash machine, or the market correctly pricing the slow death of a local-advertising business that Google's AI search and large language models are quietly disintermediating? The Q1 2026 numbers — Services advertising at +1%, the marketplace being used less each quarter, and management unable to explain how Yelp surfaces inside ChatGPT — tilt toward the second reading. The buyback can compound per-share value for a while even on a shrinking base, but it cannot reverse the secular tide.

**Economic moat:** an intangible-brand and content/network moat (330 million reviews, brand recognition in local search) that is **eroding**. The evidence is in the returns and margins: return on invested capital sits at ~9% (around or below a fair cost of capital for this risk), and although gross margin is a stable 90%, net margin halved (10% to 5%) and EBITDA margin fell (25% to 22%) in the most recent quarter, with clicks and engagement declining. A high gross margin on a shrinking, less-used marketplace is a melting asset, not a fortress.

**Secular threat — material, bordering on terminal.** The structural force is generative-AI displacement of search-and-discovery: Google holds roughly 73% of local-review share to Yelp's ~6%, about 68% of Google queries now end without a click to any outside site, and large language models like ChatGPT are becoming the new front door to local recommendations — with Yelp's own content showing up only "relatively limited" inside them. Yelp is trying to convert this threat into a data-licensing revenue stream, which is a smart hedge, but the base case is that AI search compresses the referral traffic Yelp's advertising model depends on. The cheapness is therefore better read as a structurally-shrinking base (a value-trap risk) partly offset by a strong buyback, not a clean fear-print.

# Forensic Dossier — Yelp Inc. (YELP)

*Prepared for the investment committee. Eight quarterly earnings calls reviewed (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026), cross-referenced against the screener's financial trajectory and a live balance-sheet and consensus pull as of 2026-07-10. Yelp is a local-business reviews and local-advertising platform: consumers discover restaurants and service pros; small businesses pay to advertise against that intent.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Over the last five quarters the story has quietly but decisively changed shape. In early 2025 the headline was **"services is carrying us."** Yelp had split its advertising base into two halves — Services (home and auto pros: plumbers, contractors, repair shops) and Restaurants, Retail & Other ("RR&O") — and Services was compounding at double digits (14% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2025, a sixteenth straight quarter of double-digit growth) while RR&O was shrinking. Management's message was that the strong half would outgrow the weak half and the blend would stay healthy.

That blend has since broken down. Services growth decelerated every quarter — 14% (Q1 2025) to 8% (Q2) to 7% (Q3) to roughly 1% (Q1 2026) — while RR&O's decline deepened from −3% to −11%. By the first quarter of 2026 total revenue grew just 1%. As the ad engine stalled, management pivoted the narrative hard toward **AI in two directions at once**: (1) AI-native new products — Yelp Assistant (an AI chatbot for getting quotes), Yelp Host and Yelp Receptionist (AI call-answering), and the February 2026 acquisition of Hatch (AI lead-management, growing ~92%); and (2) **data licensing** — selling Yelp's 330 million reviews and 8 million business listings to AI search players, culminating in a signed agreement with OpenAI and content appearing on Apple Maps, Amazon Alexa, Microsoft Bing and Meta.ai. The new rallying cry, repeated by the first quarter of 2026, is a target of a **$250 million annual run-rate in "other revenue" by the end of 2028** — more than double today's level.

So the arc is a company managing the slow erosion of its legacy advertising franchise by re-tooling around AI — partly as defense (its content is what AI search needs) and partly as offense (new SaaS lines). Growth drivers introduced: Yelp Assistant, Host, Hatch, licensing. Quietly de-emphasized: the old promise that Services growth alone would keep the top line healthy.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record net revenue," "strong profitability" | 2025 revenue $1.46B, up just 4%; Q1 2026 up 1% to $361M | **Poorer than it sounds** — records are set on 1–4% growth; the top line is effectively flat |
| Services is the durable growth engine | Services ad growth 14%→8%→7%→~1% across the last five quarters | **Divergent** — the engine is decelerating toward zero, not durable |
| Disciplined margins, "margin potential" | 2025 adjusted EBITDA margin 25%; but Q1 2026 net income −27% YoY, net margin 10%→5%, adjusted EBITDA −7% | **Diverging now** — 2026 is a margin-give-back year as they fund Hatch and AI |
| Aggressive buyback creating value | Fully diluted share count cut from 86M to 67M (−22%) over four years; ~$200M+ repurchased in 2025; diluted shares 62.0M (Q4 2025) → 59.4M (Q1 2026) | **Verified and material** — the single most credible value lever |
| Healthy balance sheet, capacity for deals | As of 2026-03-31: cash $110M, drew $130M long-term debt, ~$45M **net debt** (≈$20M ex-lease) | **Verified, with a correction** — the old "$300M net cash" is gone; Hatch + buybacks turned a net-cash balance sheet net-debt in one quarter |
| Other revenue is inflecting | Other revenue +75% YoY in Q1 2026 to $29M; DoorDash food-ordering +88%; Hatch run-rate $34M (+92%) | **Verified** — real, fast, but still small (~8% of revenue) |
| 90%+ gross margins | Q1 2026 gross margin fell to ~85% (cost of revenue rose as Hatch SaaS and DoorDash transactions carry real cost) | **Eroding at the edge** — the mix shift that diversifies revenue also dilutes the legendary margin |

The through-line: every favorable claim is *technically true* but sits on a top line that has gone flat, an engagement base that is shrinking, and a 2026 in which earnings actually fall. The screener's headline "Consensus forward EPS growth +39%" does **not** hold up against the live analyst file — Wall Street models 2026 earnings per share *declining* to about $1.88 (from $2.24 in 2025), then recovering to $2.62 (2027) and $3.12 (2028). Growth, not decline, but off a lower base and years out.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-defensive.** Management's tone is remarkably consistent and composed across all eight calls — no panic, no defensiveness, steady delivery. But the *content* shifted from offense to a mix of offense-and-defense:

- Q1 2025 (offense): "continued strength… strong profitability," Services "16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth."
- Q2 2025 (first hedge): advertisers "exercised increased caution," "we did not see the seasonal increase in revenue that we would typically expect."
- Q3 2025 (defensive on the core, offensive on AI): "heightened macroeconomic uncertainties will persist," lowered full-year revenue outlook — while touting "more than 35 new features" and Yelp Host.
- Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 (re-tooling): the framing became "transform Yelp with AI," "reaccelerate growth," and an explicit admission they "expect the operating environment for local businesses to remain challenging this year."

Guidance became *more* specific over time (they now give quarterly revenue and adjusted-EBITDA ranges and 2028 run-rate targets), which is a confidence tell, but the specificity is increasingly about the new AI lines rather than the core ad business.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** This is management's strongest suit. Across the reviewed quarters they consistently guided conservatively and beat — the screener records a 7-of-7 earnings-beat rate. Concrete instances: Q1 2025 revenue came in $4M above the high end of guidance and adjusted EBITDA $15M above; Q2 2025 revenue $3M above and adjusted EBITDA $11M above; Q3 2025 revenue $6M above and adjusted EBITDA $13M above; Q1 2026 revenue $6M above and adjusted EBITDA $15M above the high end. There is a clear, repeated **sandbagging pattern** — they set beatable bars, especially on adjusted EBITDA, then flow outperformance through. They also delivered exactly what they promised on flat headcount and on cutting stock-based compensation as a share of revenue (down two points a year toward the sub-8% 2025 target). The one place guidance kept *drifting down* was the full-year revenue range, which they lowered through 2025 as RR&O worsened — honest, but a reminder that the beats are against conservative bars on a weakening base.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions recur and management cannot yet answer them with numbers:

1. **"Is AI a net threat or opportunity?"** Bank of America's analyst pressed directly in Q1 2026: when you search restaurants on ChatGPT today, "Yelp content appears relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor… what needs to happen for Yelp to become more visible?" Management's answer — "we can't really comment on [OpenAI's] plans… we're even before the first inning" — is candid but is a non-answer on the single most important terminal-value question.
2. **"How big is the AI revenue, really, and when?"** Analysts repeatedly ask for the scale and timing of Yelp Host and Hatch. Management offers a "$1 billion+ TAM" and "$250M other-revenue run-rate by 2028" but declines to size near-term contribution.
3. **"Why are clicks falling if this is working?"** Ad clicks fell −3%, −7%, −11%, −10% across the last four quarters. Management attributes it to macro and to deliberately delivering "fewer but higher-quality clicks" at higher cost-per-click (CPC up 8–14%). That story works until CPC stops rising — at which point falling clicks become falling revenue.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Ad clicks down double digits** (−10% to −11% recently) and app unique devices down 2% — the consumer engagement base that feeds the whole model is shrinking, not just the RR&O segment.
🔴 **Paying advertising locations falling** — 517,000 → 485,000 over five quarters (−6% YoY in Q1 2026); the customer count is eroding across *both* segments now, not only RR&O.
🔴 **Earnings actually decline in 2026** — net income −27% YoY in Q1; consensus EPS $2.24 → ~$1.88.
🔴 **Balance sheet flipped to net debt** — $130M drawn for Hatch, net cash gone; capital-allocation optionality reduced.
🔴 **Insiders: zero open-market buys against 34 sells (476,696 shares)** — no personal conviction at these "cheap" prices; the buyback is corporate, not personal.
🔴 **Gross margin slipping** (~90% → ~85%) as the revenue mix diversifies into lower-margin lines.

🟢 **Free cash flow is enormous and real** — ~$281M trailing, a ~20% free-cash-flow yield; this is not a cash-burning turnaround.
🟢 **Buyback is aggressive and accretive** — ~11% of shares retired in two quarters, ~22% over four years; at a ~20% FCF yield each dollar of repurchase is highly value-additive.
🟢 **Other revenue +75%** with genuine AI monetization (OpenAI licensing signed, Hatch +92%, DoorDash food-ordering +88%) — the pivot is producing measurable dollars.
🟢 **Guidance credibility is high** (7/7 beats, transparent sandbagging).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The CPC-for-clicks trade is the tell.** Management has re-cast falling volume ("fewer clicks") as a feature ("higher-quality leads, higher CPC"). Revenue held because price offset volume. This is the classic late-stage move of a network whose usage is maturing — it can mask erosion for several quarters but not indefinitely.
- **"Other revenue" is being promoted from footnote to headline.** The 2028 run-rate target and the reclassification of DoorDash economics into "other revenue" signal management knows the ad line alone will not carry the story — they are re-basing investor attention onto the diversification.

*Prepared for the investment committee. Yelp is a local-business reviews and local-advertising platform: consumers discover restaurants and service pros; small businesses pay to advertise against that intent.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Over the last five quarters the story has quietly but decisively changed shape. In early 2025 the headline was **"services is carrying us."** Yelp had split its advertising base into two halves — Services (home and auto pros: plumbers, contractors, repair shops) and Restaurants, Retail & Other ("RR&O") — and Services was compounding at double digits (14% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2025, a sixteenth straight quarter of double-digit growth) while RR&O was shrinking. Management's message was that the strong half would outgrow the weak half and the blend would stay healthy.

That blend has since broken down. Services growth decelerated every quarter — 14% (Q1 2025) to 8% (Q2) to 7% (Q3) to roughly 1% (Q1 2026) — while RR&O's decline deepened from −3% to −11%. By the first quarter of 2026 total revenue grew just 1%. As the ad engine stalled, management pivoted the narrative hard toward **AI in two directions at once**: (1) AI-native new products — Yelp Assistant (an AI chatbot for getting quotes), Yelp Host and Yelp Receptionist (AI call-answering), and the February 2026 acquisition of Hatch (AI lead-management, growing ~92%); and (2) **data licensing** — selling Yelp's 330 million reviews and 8 million business listings to AI search players, culminating in a signed agreement with OpenAI and content appearing on Apple Maps, Amazon Alexa, Microsoft Bing and Meta.ai. The new rallying cry, repeated by the first quarter of 2026, is a target of a **$250 million annual run-rate in "other revenue" by the end of 2028** — more than double today's level.

So the arc is a company managing the slow erosion of its legacy advertising franchise by re-tooling around AI — partly as defense (its content is what AI search needs) and partly as offense (new SaaS lines). Growth drivers introduced: Yelp Assistant, Host, Hatch, licensing. Quietly de-emphasized: the old promise that Services growth alone would keep the top line healthy.

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |

| Services is the durable growth engine | Services ad growth 14%→8%→7%→~1% across the last five quarters | **Divergent** — the engine is decelerating toward zero, not durable |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-defensive.** Management's tone is remarkably consistent and composed across all eight calls — no panic, no defensiveness, steady delivery. But the *content* shifted from offense to a mix of offense-and-defense:

- Q1 2025 (offense): "continued strength… strong profitability," Services "16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth."
- Q2 2025 (first hedge): advertisers "exercised increased caution," "we did not see the seasonal increase in revenue that we would typically expect."
- Q3 2025 (defensive on the core, offensive on AI): "heightened macroeconomic uncertainties will persist," lowered full-year revenue outlook — while touting "more than 35 new features" and Yelp Host.
- Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 (re-tooling): the framing became "transform Yelp with AI," "reaccelerate growth," and an explicit admission they "expect the operating environment for local businesses to remain challenging this year."

Guidance became *more* specific over time (they now give quarterly revenue and adjusted-EBITDA ranges and 2028 run-rate targets), which is a confidence tell, but the specificity is increasingly about the new AI lines rather than the core ad business.

**Reliability: High.** This is management's strongest suit. Across the reviewed quarters they consistently guided conservatively and beat — the screener records a 7-of-7 earnings-beat rate. Three questions recur and management cannot yet answer them with numbers:

1. **"Is AI a net threat or opportunity?"** Bank of America's analyst pressed directly in Q1 2026: when you search restaurants on ChatGPT today, "Yelp content appears relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor… what needs to happen for Yelp to become more visible?" That story works until CPC stops rising — at which point falling clicks become falling revenue.

🔴 **Ad clicks down double digits** (−10% to −11% recently) and app unique devices down 2% — the consumer engagement base that feeds the whole model is shrinking, not just the RR&O segment.
🔴 **Paying advertising locations falling** — 517,000 → 485,000 over five quarters (−6% YoY in Q1 2026); the customer count is eroding across *both* segments now, not only RR&O.
🔴 **Earnings actually decline in 2026** — net income −27% YoY in Q1; consensus EPS $2.24 → ~$1.88.
🔴 **Balance sheet flipped to net debt** — $130M drawn for Hatch, net cash gone; capital-allocation optionality reduced.
🔴 **Insiders: zero open-market buys against 34 sells (476,696 shares)** — no personal conviction at these "cheap" prices; the buyback is corporate, not personal.
🔴 **Gross margin slipping** (~90% → ~85%) as the revenue mix diversifies into lower-margin lines.

🟢 **Free cash flow is enormous and real** — ~$281M trailing, a ~20% free-cash-flow yield; this is not a cash-burning turnaround.
🟢 **Buyback is aggressive and accretive** — ~11% of shares retired in two quarters, ~22% over four years; at a ~20% FCF yield each dollar of repurchase is highly value-additive.
🟢 **Other revenue +75%** with genuine AI monetization (OpenAI licensing signed, Hatch +92%, DoorDash food-ordering +88%) — the pivot is producing measurable dollars.
🟢 **Guidance credibility is high** (7/7 beats, transparent sandbagging).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The CPC-for-clicks trade is the tell.** Management has re-cast falling volume ("fewer clicks") as a feature ("higher-quality leads, higher CPC"). Revenue held because price offset volume. This is the classic late-stage move of a network whose usage is maturing — it can mask erosion for several quarters but not indefinitely.
- **"Other revenue" is being promoted from footnote to headline.** The 2028 run-rate target and the reclassification of DoorDash economics into "other revenue" signal management knows the ad line alone will not carry the story — they are re-basing investor attention onto the diversification.
- **The Hatch acquisition changed the capital-allocation posture.** For years the message was buyback-first with a net-cash balance sheet. Drawing debt to buy Hatch and explicitly saying margin is "not the immediate focus" for it is a real shift from harvesting to reinvesting — a bet that the AI-SaaS lines are worth more than the buyback they partly displaced.
- **Founder-CEO still in seat, still selling.** Jeremy Stoppelman remains co-founder/CEO; the consistent insider *selling* (no buys) alongside a corporate buyback is a mild governance-and-conviction tension.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** Yelp is re-tooling a maturing local-advertising franchise around AI — defensively (licensing its content to the very AI players that could disintermediate it) and offensively (Assistant, Host, Hatch). The legacy ad base is eroding at the edges (clicks, devices, locations, RR&O all down), but the company throws off a ~20% free-cash-flow yield and is shrinking the share count aggressively, so per-share value can compound even at zero top-line growth.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** whether generative-AI local search (ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity) *disintermediates Yelp's consumer traffic faster than Yelp can monetize its content through licensing and new SaaS lines.* The whole thesis is a race between two AI effects on the same company. If licensing plus Services advertising plus the new SaaS lines stabilize the base, the stock is a ~5x-free-cash-flow mispricing. If consumer traffic keeps eroding and the new lines stay sub-scale, it is a cheap-looking melting asset.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and ERODING.** The moat is an intangible-content-plus-network asset — 330 million reviews, ~500 million photos, 8 million listings that competitors cannot cheaply replicate, proven valuable by the fact that OpenAI, Apple and Amazon license it. But it was always the number-two gateway to local search behind Google, and returns-quality is holding (return on invested capital ~15%, return on equity ~20%, gross margin still high) even as the *usage base* underneath shrinks. High-but-stable returns on a slowly-shrinking traffic base is the signature of a narrow moat being eroded, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL (not yet terminal).** The structural force is generative-AI displacement of "good-enough" discovery — the risk that consumers get local answers from an AI assistant without ever visiting Yelp, collapsing the ad impressions that are ~90% of revenue. It is *material* rather than *terminal* because (a) local-services advertising still depends on lead-generation and job completion that pure chat does not yet do, (b) Yelp's content is valuable enough that the AI platforms pay to license it, giving Yelp a second monetization path, and (c) the fast-growing other-revenue line is a genuine, if partial, offset. The cheapness is therefore a **fear-print with a real thorn in it** — not a pure mispricing, but not (yet) a pure value trap either. Size it as a watch-and-accumulate value name, not an aggressive-entry catalyst play.

# Forensic Dossier — Yelp Inc. (YELP)

*Prepared for the investment committee. Eight quarterly earnings calls reviewed (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026), cross-referenced against the screener's financial trajectory and a live balance-sheet and consensus pull as of 2026-07-10. Yelp is a local-business reviews and local-advertising platform: consumers discover restaurants and service pros; small businesses pay to advertise against that intent.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Over the last five quarters the story has quietly but decisively changed shape. In early 2025 the headline was **"services is carrying us."** Yelp had split its advertising base into two halves — Services (home and auto pros: plumbers, contractors, repair shops) and Restaurants, Retail & Other ("RR&O") — and Services was compounding at double digits (14% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2025, a sixteenth straight quarter of double-digit growth) while RR&O was shrinking. Management's message was that the strong half would outgrow the weak half and the blend would stay healthy.

That blend has since broken down. Services growth decelerated every quarter — 14% (Q1 2025) to 8% (Q2) to 7% (Q3) to roughly 1% (Q1 2026) — while RR&O's decline deepened from −3% to −11%. By the first quarter of 2026 total revenue grew just 1%. As the ad engine stalled, management pivoted the narrative hard toward **AI in two directions at once**: (1) AI-native new products — Yelp Assistant (an AI chatbot for getting quotes), Yelp Host and Yelp Receptionist (AI call-answering), and the February 2026 acquisition of Hatch (AI lead-management, growing ~92%); and (2) **data licensing** — selling Yelp's 330 million reviews and 8 million business listings to AI search players, culminating in a signed agreement with OpenAI and content appearing on Apple Maps, Amazon Alexa, Microsoft Bing and Meta.ai. The new rallying cry, repeated by the first quarter of 2026, is a target of a **$250 million annual run-rate in "other revenue" by the end of 2028** — more than double today's level.

So the arc is a company managing the slow erosion of its legacy advertising franchise by re-tooling around AI — partly as defense (its content is what AI search needs) and partly as offense (new SaaS lines). Growth drivers introduced: Yelp Assistant, Host, Hatch, licensing. Quietly de-emphasized: the old promise that Services growth alone would keep the top line healthy.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record net revenue," "strong profitability" | 2025 revenue $1.46B, up just 4%; Q1 2026 up 1% to $361M | **Poorer than it sounds** — records are set on 1–4% growth; the top line is effectively flat |
| Services is the durable growth engine | Services ad growth 14%→8%→7%→~1% across the last five quarters | **Divergent** — the engine is decelerating toward zero, not durable |
| Disciplined margins, "margin potential" | 2025 adjusted EBITDA margin 25%; but Q1 2026 net income −27% YoY, net margin 10%→5%, adjusted EBITDA −7% | **Diverging now** — 2026 is a margin-give-back year as they fund Hatch and AI |
| Aggressive buyback creating value | Fully diluted share count cut from 86M to 67M (−22%) over four years; ~$200M+ repurchased in 2025; diluted shares 62.0M (Q4 2025) → 59.4M (Q1 2026) | **Verified and material** — the single most credible value lever |
| Healthy balance sheet, capacity for deals | As of 2026-03-31: cash $110M, drew $130M long-term debt, ~$45M **net debt** (≈$20M ex-lease) | **Verified, with a correction** — the old "$300M net cash" is gone; Hatch + buybacks turned a net-cash balance sheet net-debt in one quarter |
| Other revenue is inflecting | Other revenue +75% YoY in Q1 2026 to $29M; DoorDash food-ordering +88%; Hatch run-rate $34M (+92%) | **Verified** — real, fast, but still small (~8% of revenue) |
| 90%+ gross margins | Q1 2026 gross margin fell to ~85% (cost of revenue rose as Hatch SaaS and DoorDash transactions carry real cost) | **Eroding at the edge** — the mix shift that diversifies revenue also dilutes the legendary margin |

The through-line: every favorable claim is *technically true* but sits on a top line that has gone flat, an engagement base that is shrinking, and a 2026 in which earnings actually fall. The screener's headline "Consensus forward EPS growth +39%" does **not** hold up against the live analyst file — Wall Street models 2026 earnings per share *declining* to about $1.88 (from $2.24 in 2025), then recovering to $2.62 (2027) and $3.12 (2028). Growth, not decline, but off a lower base and years out.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-defensive.** Management's tone is remarkably consistent and composed across all eight calls — no panic, no defensiveness, steady delivery. But the *content* shifted from offense to a mix of offense-and-defense:

- Q1 2025 (offense): "continued strength… strong profitability," Services "16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth."
- Q2 2025 (first hedge): advertisers "exercised increased caution," "we did not see the seasonal increase in revenue that we would typically expect."
- Q3 2025 (defensive on the core, offensive on AI): "heightened macroeconomic uncertainties will persist," lowered full-year revenue outlook — while touting "more than 35 new features" and Yelp Host.
- Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 (re-tooling): the framing became "transform Yelp with AI," "reaccelerate growth," and an explicit admission they "expect the operating environment for local businesses to remain challenging this year."

Guidance became *more* specific over time (they now give quarterly revenue and adjusted-EBITDA ranges and 2028 run-rate targets), which is a confidence tell, but the specificity is increasingly about the new AI lines rather than the core ad business.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** This is management's strongest suit. Across the reviewed quarters they consistently guided conservatively and beat — the screener records a 7-of-7 earnings-beat rate. Concrete instances: Q1 2025 revenue came in $4M above the high end of guidance and adjusted EBITDA $15M above; Q2 2025 revenue $3M above and adjusted EBITDA $11M above; Q3 2025 revenue $6M above and adjusted EBITDA $13M above; Q1 2026 revenue $6M above and adjusted EBITDA $15M above the high end. There is a clear, repeated **sandbagging pattern** — they set beatable bars, especially on adjusted EBITDA, then flow outperformance through. They also delivered exactly what they promised on flat headcount and on cutting stock-based compensation as a share of revenue (down two points a year toward the sub-8% 2025 target). ## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions recur and management cannot yet answer them with numbers:

1. **"Is AI a net threat or opportunity?"** Bank of America's analyst pressed directly in Q1 2026: when you search restaurants on ChatGPT today, "Yelp content appears relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor… what needs to happen for Yelp to become more visible?" Management's answer — "we can't really comment on [OpenAI's] plans… we're even before the first inning" — is candid but is a non-answer on the single most important terminal-value question.
2. **"How big is the AI revenue, really, and when?"** Analysts repeatedly ask for the scale and timing of Yelp Host and Hatch. Management offers a "$1 billion+ TAM" and "$250M other-revenue run-rate by 2028" but declines to size near-term contribution.
3. **"Why are clicks falling if this is working?"** Ad clicks fell −3%, −7%, −11%, −10% across the last four quarters. Management attributes it to macro and to deliberately delivering "fewer but higher-quality clicks" at higher cost-per-click (CPC up 8–14%). ## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Ad clicks down double digits** (−10% to −11% recently) and app unique devices down 2% — the consumer engagement base that feeds the whole model is shrinking, not just the RR&O segment.
🔴 **Paying advertising locations falling** — 517,000 → 485,000 over five quarters (−6% YoY in Q1 2026); the customer count is eroding across *both* segments now, not only RR&O.
🔴 **Earnings actually decline in 2026** — net income −27% YoY in Q1; consensus EPS $2.24 → ~$1.88.
🔴 **Balance sheet flipped to net debt** — $130M drawn for Hatch, net cash gone; capital-allocation optionality reduced.
🔴 **Insiders: zero open-market buys against 34 sells (476,696 shares)** — no personal conviction at these "cheap" prices; the buyback is corporate, not personal.
🔴 **Gross margin slipping** (~90% → ~85%) as the revenue mix diversifies into lower-margin lines.

🟢 **Free cash flow is enormous and real** — ~$281M trailing, a ~20% free-cash-flow yield; this is not a cash-burning turnaround.
🟢 **Buyback is aggressive and accretive** — ~11% of shares retired in two quarters, ~22% over four years; at a ~20% FCF yield each dollar of repurchase is highly value-additive.
🟢 **Other revenue +75%** with genuine AI monetization (OpenAI licensing signed, Hatch +92%, DoorDash food-ordering +88%) — the pivot is producing measurable dollars.
🟢 **Guidance credibility is high** (7/7 beats, transparent sandbagging).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The CPC-for-clicks trade is the tell.** Management has re-cast falling volume ("fewer clicks") as a feature ("higher-quality leads, higher CPC"). Revenue held because price offset volume. This is the classic late-stage move of a network whose usage is maturing — it can mask erosion for several quarters but not indefinitely.
- **"Other revenue" is being promoted from footnote to headline.** The 2028 run-rate target and the reclassification of DoorDash economics into "other revenue" signal management knows the ad line alone will not carry the story — they are re-basing investor attention onto the diversification.
- **The Hatch acquisition changed the capital-allocation posture.** For years the message was buyback-first with a net-cash balance sheet. Drawing debt to buy Hatch and explicitly saying margin is "not the immediate focus" for it is a real shift from harvesting to reinvesting — a bet that the AI-SaaS lines are worth more than the buyback they partly displaced.
- **Founder-CEO still in seat, still selling.** Jeremy Stoppelman remains co-founder/CEO; the consistent insider *selling* (no buys) alongside a corporate buyback is a mild governance-and-conviction tension.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** Yelp is re-tooling a maturing local-advertising franchise around AI — defensively (licensing its content to the very AI players that could disintermediate it) and offensively (Assistant, Host, Hatch). The legacy ad base is eroding at the edges (clicks, devices, locations, RR&O all down), but the company throws off a ~20% free-cash-flow yield and is shrinking the share count aggressively, so per-share value can compound even at zero top-line growth.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** whether generative-AI local search (ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity) *disintermediates Yelp's consumer traffic faster than Yelp can monetize its content through licensing and new SaaS lines.* The whole thesis is a race between two AI effects on the same company. If licensing plus Services advertising plus the new SaaS lines stabilize the base, the stock is a ~5x-free-cash-flow mispricing. If consumer traffic keeps eroding and the new lines stay sub-scale, it is a cheap-looking melting asset.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and ERODING.** The moat is an intangible-content-plus-network asset — 330 million reviews, ~500 million photos, 8 million listings that competitors cannot cheaply replicate, proven valuable by the fact that OpenAI, Apple and Amazon license it. But it was always the number-two gateway to local search behind Google, and returns-quality is holding (return on invested capital ~15%, return on equity ~20%, gross margin still high) even as the *usage base* underneath shrinks. High-but-stable returns on a slowly-shrinking traffic base is the signature of a narrow moat being eroded, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL (not yet terminal).** The structural force is generative-AI displacement of "good-enough" discovery — the risk that consumers get local answers from an AI assistant without ever visiting Yelp, collapsing the ad impressions that are ~90% of revenue. It is *material* rather than *terminal* because (a) local-services advertising still depends on lead-generation and job completion that pure chat does not yet do, (b) Yelp's content is valuable enough that the AI platforms pay to license it, giving Yelp a second monetization path, and (c) the fast-growing other-revenue line is a genuine, if partial, offset. The cheapness is therefore a **fear-print with a real thorn in it** — not a pure mispricing, but not (yet) a pure value trap either. Size it as a watch-and-accumulate value name, not an aggressive-entry catalyst play.
